source.title: No Free Lunch From Random Feature Ensembles
source.authors: Benjamin S. Ruben; W. Tong; H. Chaudhry; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.tranche_reason: The study reports scaling results for random-feature ridge regression, including experiments on image-classification datasets; this is an extension to a different model and task setting, not a test of language-model pretraining laws.
record.gate_note: The study does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling for language models, or downstream performance after language-model pretraining. Its own random-feature test-risk scaling results bear on V5 as a different training/model setting. Results it cites about language-model scaling are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyses random-feature ridge regression (RFRR) ensembles, a kernel toy model, not neural language models or neural models in other modalities. Its power-law test-risk results come from two places. On synthetic tasks the power-law kernel spectra and target weights are imposed by construction, so the risk power law follows from the assumptions. On binarized CIFAR-10 and MNIST, theory-predicted exponents are checked against simulated RFRR. None of this measures whether the scaling-law versions hold for the kind of system they name: V1–V4, V6 and V7 concern LM pretraining, and V5 concerns neural models in other modalities or regimes. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in the discussion, as context. I record the RFRR scaling results under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. In RFRR with optimally tuned ridge, the authors prove that more data, more features and more ensemble members never increase risk. For a fixed total feature count, a single model is optimal and risk rises with K. Overparameterized ensembles are near-optimal because, at leading order, risk depends only on KN. Under joint growth of K and N, the scaling exponent depends on ℓ and task eigenstructure. Near-optimal scaling is possible for easy tasks (r>1/2) when ℓ exceeds a threshold.
record.recipe_differences: Uses deterministic-equivalent risk analysis and random-feature ridge regression, with test MSE and total feature count as the principal quantities; it does not use language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling depends on task eigenstructure (α and r), growth exponent ℓ, whether the task is underparameterized or overparameterized, and ridge choice. The study reports that near-optimal scaling under joint ensemble/model growth depends on task difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: In RFRR ensembles, test MSE scales as M^-s in total feature count. The exponent s depends on the task's source and capacity exponents and on the growth exponent ℓ. Predicted exponents match simulations on synthetic power-law tasks and on binarized CIFAR-10 and MNIST (Figs 4, 5). The optimal exponent is always reached at ℓ=1, i.e. a single model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In random-feature kernel models, power-law test-risk scaling with feature count is predicted by the kernel and target eigenstructure, and splitting features across ensemble members never improves the exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: In the overparameterized regime with small ridge, risk depends on K and N only through KN at leading order (eq. 24).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterized random-feature ensembles perform close to a single model of equal total size.

record.problems: The results concern random-feature ridge regression rather than language models and use test MSE rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy. The Gaussian universality assumption is used; the text notes that deterministic-equivalence results have not been proven for ensembled RFRR (K>1). Numerical scaling results are presented for synthetic tasks and binarized image datasets.

untested.parts: All: no extrapolation from small to large LM runs.
All: no compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens. The ensemble-versus-single-model allocation studied here is a different question.
All: no test of architecture shape at fixed parameter count in LMs.
All: no neural image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. Only kernel RFRR toy models are studied.
All: no examination of how published LM laws depend on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'supports' label is removed. The system is a kernel toy model, not the kind of system V5 names. On synthetic tasks the power law is built into the assumptions. On the image tasks, the predicted exponents rest on spectra that were themselves fitted to power laws. The study's link to Kaplan and Hoffmann is discussion only.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between language-model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of language-model architecture shape at fixed parameter count.

Language-model regimes beyond text pretraining, including image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer. This study tests random-feature ridge regression, including on image-classification tasks, not those model types or regimes.
Downstream performance after language-model pretraining, or its relation to language-model pretraining loss.
Dependence of the original language-model laws on parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method; disagreement between those laws; and bending of language-model curves.

rows.subject: linear random-feature regression (synthetic Gaussian data)
rows.size_stated: N features per ensemble member; K members; total feature count M=KN
rows.operation_detail: Jointly scaled ensemble size K and features per member N with total feature count M; measured test risk scaling.

conditions.value: synthetic Gaussian data with power-law eigenstructure

rows.measure: Test risk EgK versus total feature count M; predicted power-law exponent s=min(2αℓ min(r,1), 1−ℓ+2αℓ min(r,1/2)).
rows.value: For r<1/2, the bias dominates and the scaling exponent increases linearly with ℓ; the predicted scaling laws agree with numerical simulations.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 4 simulations; no numerical uncertainty stated in the text.
rows.note: The text describes r=0.4 as a difficult-task regime; Figure 4 compares theoretical scaling exponents with fitted simulation results.
rows.check: Linear Gaussian random-feature regression on a synthetic task whose power-law spectrum (α=1.5, r=0.4) is imposed by construction. This is not a neural model in another modality, and the power law follows from the assumed eigenstructure. The row is also about how the exponent depends on the growth exponent ℓ, not about whether a power law holds.

rows.subject: ReLU random-feature ridge regression on binarized CIFAR-10
rows.size_stated: Total feature count M varied; K and N jointly scaled
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-risk scaling with total feature count at optimally chosen ridge; compared predicted and empirical scaling exponents.
rows.measure: Test risk versus M and empirical power-law scaling exponent.
rows.value: The task is in the difficult regime r<1/2; predicted scaling exponents agree with empirical scaling laws.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5 shows simulation error bars; the text does not state their numerical values.
rows.note: The reported α and r are estimates from the NNGP kernel spectrum and target weights; the empirical fitted risk exponent is not numerically stated in the text.
rows.check: ReLU RFRR (a kernel method with fixed random features) on binarized CIFAR-10. The test MSE power law in feature count is compared with exponents predicted from spectra already fitted to power laws. It is not a trained neural image model, so it does not bear on V5. No fitted exponent value is given in the text.

conditions.value: small; expansion to leading order in λ and 1/N

rows.measure: Leading-order test-risk dependence on ensemble size and model size.
rows.value: At leading order, risk depends on K and N only through total feature count KN; the expression includes a term proportional to 1/(KN).
rows.locator: Section 6.1, equation 24; Appendix D.2, equations D.20–D.23
rows.note: This is an analytical random-feature result, not an empirical measurement of language-model loss.
rows.check: Analytical expansion (eq. 24) showing that risk depends on K and N only through KN at leading order. This is a derived result, not an empirical scaling measurement. It concerns how ensemble members are allocated, not a power law in scale.
